title: When Teacher Training Feels Like a Sales Pitch (and How to Push Back)
author: Jim Hewitt and Nidhi Sachdeva
summary: Jim Hewitt and Nidhi Sachdeva identify five persuasive moves that can turn well-intentioned professional development into something closer to a sales pitch: invoking "research says" without specifying study quality, "trust the expert" appeals to eminent names (from Vygotsky to today's edu-celebrities), loaded language that stigmatises evidence-based practices like retrieval practice as "drill and kill" while romanticising vaguer ones, using equity as a blanket justification that shuts down scrutiny, and leaning on theory as though it were evidence. For each move they offer specific, low-confrontation questions teachers can ask to redirect the conversation back toward evidence, arguing the goal is not combativeness but keeping professional learning honest and centred on what actually helps students learn.
points: The five persuasive moves -- "research says," trust-the-expert, loaded language, the equity justification, and all-theory-no-evidence -- function as an anatomy of how well-intentioned CPD slides into unfalsifiable rhetoric.

Their loaded-language example is the sharpest: retrieval practice and explicit instruction are well-evidenced (citing Agarwal, Nunes & Blunt 2021; Kirschner, Sweller & Clark 2006) yet routinely get dismissed via labels like "drill and kill" or "sage on the stage."

On equity, they distinguish between well-evidenced claims that specific practices narrow achievement gaps and the rhetorical move of fusing a practice with the goal of equity itself so that questioning the practice reads as not caring about equity.

Each of the five sections ends with concrete, non-confrontational questions teachers can ask in the room -- e.g., "Can you share the study?" or "How does that thinker's work apply to this specific instructional practice?" -- making the piece directly usable rather than just diagnostic.
quotes: Certain approaches were presented as the only right ones. Others were brushed aside with a dismissive label.
The problem is that “research says” is sometimes used to make an idea sound more authoritative than it really is.
Paul Kirschner and Mirjam Neelen refer to this as eminence-based education. The problem? It discourages questions.

Retrieval practice and explicit instruction, for example, are highly effective for novice learners (Agarwal, Nunes, & Blunt, 2021; Kirschner, Sweller, & Clark, 2006). Yet if you say you use retrieval practice, you risk being accused of “drill and kill.
Sometimes practices criticized as inequitable, like explicit instruction, have in fact been shown to support struggling learners (Hattie, 2009; Stockard et al., 2018).
Pushing back doesn’t mean being combative. It means keeping the dialogue honest, evidence-informed, and centred on student learning.
